transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Jonah Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Orion), Marcus Lee (Orion), Ava Gomez (Orion)

---
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, joining today with Jonah our SE. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya Sharma: Hi Priya here.
[00:10] Marcus Lee: Marcus.
[00:11] Ava Gomez: Ava here.
[00:13] Jonah Rivera: Jonah -- SE. Thanks for making time.
[00:16] Lena Park: Great. Agenda — short demo of the SDKs (Python and TypeScript), auth/env setup, quick Console tour and a couple tips from Redwood Optimize for cost/latency. Then Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Priya Sharma: Yep, sounds good. We're mostly interested in integration patterns and streaming. Also curious re: private deployment options.
[00:34] Jonah Rivera: Perfect, I'll share my screen and start with the Python quickstart.
[00:41] [00:41] Jonah Rivera: Okay, so here is the repo — it's called redwood-sdk-quickstart, go to examples/python/streaming.py, quick note on install: pip install redwood-inference (note: earlier we called it redwood-sdk in docs but the package is redwood-inference).
[00:55] Marcus Lee: Small question — is auth via a single API key or do you support service accounts?
[01:01] Jonah Rivera: Good call out. We support API key for hosted, and for Dedicated/Private you can do service account tokens and KMS-backed keys. In the SDK we read env var REDWOOD_API_KEY by default, you can also supply a credentials object.
[01:15] Priya Sharma: Is SSO or SAML part of that?
[01:18] Lena Park: Yes, SSO is through the Console for user access; for machine auth you use service accounts with scoped roles. We'll share the security doc.
[01:27] [01:27] Jonah Rivera: Back to code — streaming example uses client.stream_chat with an async iterator, you get partial tokens as they arrive. Example:
[01:37] Jonah Rivera: """ python snippet (transcript paraphrase)
from redwood_inference import Client
client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
async for chunk in client.stream_chat(model='rw-medium', prompt='...'):
    print(chunk.text)
"""
[01:58] Ava Gomez: That model name, rw-medium, is that Redwood's internal name?
[02:02] Jonah Rivera: It's shorthand — our catalog maps to curated open models and variants; in Console you'll see the verified performance profile. Sometimes the transcript will show rw-med or rw medium, tooling glitches.
[02:14] [02:14] Marcus Lee: For TypeScript, is it basically the same?
[02:16] Jonah Rivera: Yep, npm i @redwood/inference or npm i redwood-inference-js (we have a few published names, docs link will be precise). Example:
[02:25] Jonah Rivera: """ ts paraphrase
import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
for await (const chunk of client.streamChat({ model: 'rw-medium', prompt })) {
  console.log(chunk.text)
}
"""
[02:48] Priya Sharma: Great. About environment setup: we want to pin versions and guarantee reproducible installs, any guidance?
[02:55] Jonah Rivera: We recommend pinning both SDK and model versions in your lockfile, and using model version pins in the request (model: 'rw-medium@v1.2'). That lets rollouts happen without surprises. Also for reproducible infra, Dedicated gives you a fixed GPU fleet.
[03:09] [03:09] Lena Park: Quick Console peek — I'll switch to Lena's screen — shows project, API keys, usage, and routes. The Console has per-route dashboards, token breakdowns and tracing hooks.
[03:23] Priya Sharma: Does Console show per-token cost by model?
[03:26] Lena Park: Yes, you can filter by model/route and see token breakdown and cost estimates; Redwood Optimize will propose batching or quantization adjustments per workload.
[03:36] [03:36] Marcus Lee: We're concerned about PII and data retention. How long do you retain logs for hosted? Can we disable retention?
[03:44] Lena Park: Hosted by default retains minimal logs for 30 days, longer with enterprise packages. For Private you control retention. We support audit logs, SSO and KMS. We'll attach the SOC 2 and ISO summary.
[03:58] [03:58] Priya Sharma: Nice. For streaming and latency — what p95 numbers do people see for 256-token prompts?
[04:06] Jonah Rivera: It depends on model and deployment. Hosted with rw-medium we often see p95 around 200-350ms for generation time per token in optimized paths; end-to-end can be a few hundred ms depending on network. Dedicated can be optimized further, and Optimize suggests batching/caching profiles.
[04:22] Ava Gomez: Do you have a recommended causal cache configuration for conversational apps?
[04:26] Jonah Rivera: Yes, use prefix KV caching in the runtime and enable prefix-based routing, prevents re-computing the same prefix for subsequent requests — huge win for chat apps. We'll share docs and the Optimize recommendations.
[04:39] [04:39] Marcus Lee: Any gotchas for Node serverless environments?
[04:43] Jonah Rivera: Watch cold start and connection reuse — use the SDK client as a singleton, keep connections warm with a lightweight ping if you have strict latency SLOs. Also be careful with streaming in some FaaS platforms that time out; we show patterns in the quickstart.
[04:58] Priya Sharma: For RBAC, can we have per-route service accounts with limited scopes?
[05:02] Lena Park: Yes, Console supports per-route keys and scoped service accounts in Private/Dedicated. Hosted has role-scoped tokens too — we'll add the matrix to the security doc.
[05:12] [05:12] Jonah Rivera: Now switching back to code — authentication patterns: simplest is export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-... in your env; for CI use secrets manager integrations (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) and for Private we integrate with your KMS.
[05:28] Priya Sharma: Can we rotate keys without downtime?
[05:30] Jonah Rivera: Yes, we recommend issuing a new key and updating your deployment; keys are versioned and you can revoke old keys. For Dedicated you can do key rotation via Console and API.
[05:41] [05:41] Ava Gomez: About private deployments, what's the typical timeline for VPC setup?
[05:45] Lena Park: For Private VPC the usual is 6-8 weeks depending on network approvals, for Dedicated it's faster — typically 2-4 weeks. If you're onprem it can take longer. We'll need a network contact to share the VPC peering details.
[05:58] Marcus Lee: Any compliance controls for health data?
[06:01] Lena Park: We have enterprise packages and on-prem options with customer-managed keys and audit trails; we'll share the compliance pack.
[06:10] [06:10] Priya Sharma: Can you show the TypeScript streaming with function/tool-calling?
[06:15] Jonah Rivera: Sure, this is a simplified snippet — we support function calling patterns; the SDK exposes a tools param and the model can return structured JSON you can validate. Example paraphrase: client.chat({ tools: [ { name: 'lookup_patient', schema: {...} } ] })
[06:33] Priya Sharma: How are semantics for function-calling validated? Is there schema enforcement?
[06:37] Jonah Rivera: We do basic schema validation in the runtime and recommend post-validate on your side. The Console can show structured outputs in logs.
[06:47] [06:47] Marcus Lee: Cost questions — if we do 1M requests/month with avg tokens X, what are the levers to reduce cost?
[06:52] Lena Park: The big levers: batching, KV/prefix caching, using quantized model variants, and picking model family by quality need. Redwood Optimize can simulate cost impact of batching and propose config changes. We'll run a quick cost sim in the POC.
[07:09] [07:09] Ava Gomez: Is there a trial or credit for POC?
[07:12] Lena Park: Yes, we offer POC credits and can put you on a trial Dedicated pool for benchmarking. I'll include POC terms in the email.
[07:20] Jonah Rivera: Quick note on error handling — SDK surfaces typed errors, transient errors auto-retry based on policy, and you can set a per-request fallback to a cheaper model.
[07:33] Priya Sharma: Nice. For logs we need UPN and correlation IDs. Are those available?
[07:38] Lena Park: Yes, you can pass a request_id and user_id in metadata and Console/traces will surface those.
[07:45] [07:45] Marcus Lee: Any customers in health we can reference?
[07:48] Lena Park: We have a couple NDA'd customers; we'll share redacted case studies.
[07:53] [07:53] Priya Sharma: Ok, let's talk next steps.
[07:56] Lena Park: Recap: we'll send the quickstart repo, security/compliance docs, and sample streaming snippets. Jonah will prepare Python + TS streaming demos and a small benchmark script. You (Priya) will share prompts and latency targets, and we'll schedule a technical POC next week.
[08:14] Ava Gomez: Sounds good.
[08:16] [08:16] Priya Sharma: One more question — do you support on-prem GPUs with custom kernels?
[08:20] Jonah Rivera: We support on-prem with our Private package; kernel selection is part of our runtime, we bring a compiled runtime that targets your hardware, we do kernel tuning during onboarding. Sometimes our docs call it kernel selector or compile step — transcripts sometimes render that oddly.
[08:37] Marcus Lee: Are there limits to model parallelism in Dedicated?
[08:40] Jonah Rivera: You can configure instance sizes and job-level parallelism; we'll share the Dedicated capacity guide.
[08:47] [08:47] Lena Park: All right, last bits — we'll follow up with links and schedule. Thanks everyone.
[08:54] Ava Gomez: Thanks all.
[08:56] [08:56] (call ends)
